title: ‘Well beyond warnings’: ASIC tightens the screws on private credit funds
full_text:
Private credit managers are “well beyond warnings”, according to ASIC, as it urges them to improve practices by the end of the year.
Speaking at the Commercial & Asset Finance Brokers of Australia (CAFBA) Commercial Property & Development Finance Summit in Sydney on 22 September, ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the watchdog had shone a light on weaknesses in private credit, but too many had been slow to respond.
ASIC’s work so far has included a surveillance of 28 private credit funds which identified a number of ‘red flags’ such as how only four published information about the interest rates or ranges charged to borrowers, less than half had detailed credit or impairment and default management policies in place and most funds lacked adequate separation between those approving loans and those responsible for independently assessing their ongoing performance and value.
A subsequent report assessed Australia’s private market performance against global peers and found Australia fell beneath comparable jurisdictions like Singapore and the US.
Following these two reports, ASIC put together 10 guiding principles to demonstrate best practice.
The regulator had previously challenged firms to improve their practices by the end of 2027 as part of its thematic and surveillance work but Constant said not all had heeded its call. If fund managers are still unable to meet the regulator’s standards, Constant said enforcement action would be next on the list.
“We challenged the sector to lift standards by 2027 – and that’s only three months away.
“So as an industry, you need to drive this change – because if you don’t, ASIC may be forced to do it for you, through regulatory and enforcement action.
“If you are a private credit fund who hasn’t assessed yourself against the 10 principles of private credit done well that we published, again ask yourselves – why not? Before your investors do.
“Get things wrong and you could be facing disputes and litigation – and your boards will be wishing they’d included private credit principles as a standing item on their agenda.”
Bathla collapse
This is exacerbated by factors such as the collapse of property developer Bathla Group which went into administration in August owing $3 billion. While Constant said this was “deeply concerning”, she said she was unsurprised by its occurrence as the system came under pressure.
Real estate lending accounts for 40-60 per cent of private credit in Australia and has been described as “the weakest link” in the sector as it is vulnerable to a wide range of factors such as inflation, cost escalation, project delays and interest rate rises.
“As we’ve seen with Bathla, developers with exposure to private credit are particularly vulnerable when economic conditions become more challenging. It’s one of the reasons why good governance, effective controls and industry standards are crucial.
“What we’re seeing now, as some of those weaknesses are tested at scale for the first time in current conditions, are the first significant cracks – the first stress fractures – beginning to emerge.
“To avoid these stress fractures becoming a stressed system, the sector must lift its standards and maintain them, consistently.
“Whether we see broader credit stress or not, certainly the tide is going out on poorer private credit practices. The collapse of Bathla reinforces why strong governance, effective oversight, clear disclosure and accurate valuations are critical.”
